## Proof

In a Dedekind domain, every nonzero proper ideal admits a unique factorization into prime ideals. Let

$$I = \prod_{\mathfrak{q}} \mathfrak{q}^{a_{\mathfrak{q}}}, \qquad J = \prod_{\mathfrak{q}} \mathfrak{q}^{b_{\mathfrak{q}}}$$

where the products range over prime ideals, $a_{\mathfrak{q}}, b_{\mathfrak{q}} \geq 0$, and only finitely many exponents are nonzero.

**Divisibility and LCM in Dedekind domains.** For nonzero ideals, $I \mid J$ (i.e., there exists an ideal $A$ with $IA = J$) if and only if $J \subseteq I$, which holds if and only if $a_{\mathfrak{q}} \leq b_{\mathfrak{q}}$ for every prime $\mathfrak{q}$. The least common multiple of $I$ and $J$ — the smallest ideal (under divisibility) divisible by both — is therefore

$$\operatorname{lcm}(I, J) = \prod_{\mathfrak{q}} \mathfrak{q}^{\max(a_{\mathfrak{q}},\, b_{\mathfrak{q}})}.$$

**Applying the hypothesis.** We are given $\operatorname{lcm}(I, J) = P^{k}$. By unique factorization, this forces

$$\max(a_{\mathfrak{q}},\, b_{\mathfrak{q}}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathfrak{q} \neq P, \qquad \max(a_{P},\, b_{P}) = k.$$

The first condition gives $a_{\mathfrak{q}} = b_{\mathfrak{q}} = 0$ for all $\mathfrak{q} \neq P$, so both $I$ and $J$ are powers of $P$ alone:

$$I = P^{a_P}, \qquad J = P^{b_P}.$$

The second condition gives $\max(a_P, b_P) = k$ with $a_P, b_P \geq 0$. Since $k \geq 1$ (as $P^k$ is a proper nonzero ideal), at least one of $a_P, b_P$ equals $k$:

- If $a_P = k$, then $I = P^k$.
- If $b_P = k$, then $J = P^k$.

(It is possible that both equal $k$, in which case $I = J = P^k$.)

**Conclusion.** Yes, it necessarily follows that either $I = P^k$ or $J = P^k$. $\blacksquare$
